How much of the pipeline succeeded — the trust signal for consumers.

Downstream agents (Copilot/Claude/tools) read ``level`` to decide whether to
act confidently, act cautiously, or ask the user for more evidence instead of
fabricating a fix from a near-empty bundle.

Structured "what to build" context for feature / build / demo / design videos.

This is the build counterpart to the bug-oriented fields. It gives a coding
agent a buildable model of the video — screens, components, the user flow
between them, design notes, and where in the codebase to implement — instead
of a flat caption + OCR blob.

first-class build assistant, not only a bug fixer.

ContextBundle.description:
The canonical output: complete structured context extracted from a video.

Framesleuth works on *any* video — a bug recording, a feature demo, a design
walkthrough, a Loom, a phone capture — and distills it into this single
structured artifact a coding agent can act on: to fix a bug, add or change a
feature, or build something new. Bug-oriented fields (``severity``,
``priority``, ``suspected_component``) double as generic triage signals for
non-bug work (how urgent/important the task is and where it lives in the code).

This is the primary artifact delivered to both VS Code and Chrome surfaces.
Schema versioning enables forward migration and compatibility checks.

Bug-oriented fields (``severity``, ``priority``, ``suspected_component``,
``preconditions``, ``repro_steps``, ``expected_behavior``,
``actual_behavior``, ``reproducibility``) are populated only when the video
actually depicts a defect (a ``bug`` classification or real error evidence).
For a general video — a demo, a walkthrough, a real-world clip — they are
``None``/empty and the deliverable is the ``summary`` plus ``key_moments``.

ErrorBody.description:
The body of every non-2xx response.

This is the WHOLE body, not a nested field. The API installs exception
handlers that flatten FastAPI's default ``{"detail": {...}}`` wrapper, so a
client reads ``code`` directly off the response.

``code`` is the stable, machine-readable discriminator (see
:class:`framesleuth.errors.ErrorCode`); ``error`` is human text, ``hint`` an
optional actionable next step, and ``request_id`` matches the
``X-Request-ID`` response header so one value ties a report to its logs.
Clients should branch on ``code``.

request_id.description: Correlation id, also returned as the X-Request-ID header

KeyMoment.description:
A salient, timestamped moment in the recording.

The building block of a general-video *analysis*: a short, time-anchored
description of what happens at a point in the video (a scene change, an
action, a spoken point, or an error). Derived deterministically from the
fused video + audio timeline, so it carries an evidence citation and never
fabricates.

Provenance.description:
What produced this bundle.

Without it, a bundle is unattributable: a quality regression after a prompt
edit or a model swap cannot be traced to either, and eval results cannot be
tied to the prompts that produced them. ``repo_root``/``git_commit`` matter
for a different reason — ``code_candidates`` are ``file:line`` pairs, and a
line number is meaningless a week later unless you know which commit it was
resolved against.

RenderHtmlRequest.description:
``POST /v1/render-html`` — an HTML animation to capture as a clip.

Fields are intentionally *unconstrained* here. The renderer
(``RenderOptions.normalized``) is the single authority on what is a valid
combination, and it reports problems as the documented
``missing_html`` / ``bad_options`` / ``html_too_large`` codes. Duplicating
those bounds as Pydantic constraints would turn every one of them into a
generic 422 and split the contract across two places.
RenderHtmlRequest.title: RenderHtmlRequest

post.description:
Accept a recording and queue it for analysis.

Returns ``202`` with the new ``job_id`` immediately; the analysis runs in
the background (bounded by ``MAX_CONCURRENT_JOBS``). Poll ``/v1/jobs/{id}``
for progress and ``/v1/report/{id}`` once the state is ``done``.

get.description:
Render (and cache) an animated GIF preview of the recording.

The client embeds this looping preview wherever a video player is awkward
(issues, chat, the extension popup). Query params ``fps``/``width``/
``start``/``end`` are optional and clamped to safe ranges; results are
cached on disk per parameter set, so repeat requests are served instantly.

Report dependency readiness and the live queue depth.

Public even when ``API_TOKEN`` is set, so a client can tell "backend is
down" from "backend needs a token" before authenticating.

List jobs, newest first, with pagination and state filtering.

Lets a client browse analysis history — and ask for just the failed or
just the running ones — instead of paging everything and filtering
client-side.

delete.description:
Request cooperative cancellation of a running/queued job.

The pipeline checks the cancel flag at each stage boundary and transitions
to ``cancelled``. Already-terminal jobs are returned unchanged (``409``).

409.description: Job is not in a valid state for this call

get.description: Return one job's lifecycle state, progress, and per-stage metrics.

Stream job progress as Server-Sent Events until a terminal state.

Each event is a JSON snapshot (`state`, `progress_pct`); the stream closes
once the job is `done`/`failed`/`cancelled`. Lets a client follow progress
without polling.

post.description:
Render an HTML document (CSS / JS / canvas animation) to a clip.

Synchronous — returns the encoded file. Requires the optional ``render``
extra (Playwright) and ``ffmpeg``; returns ``503`` with an actionable
message when unavailable.

delete.description:
Delete a finished report: its bundle directory and the job row.

On-demand purge so a user isn't forced to wait for the TTL sweep. Only
terminal jobs can be deleted — an active job must be cancelled first
(``DELETE /v1/jobs/{id}``) so its running pipeline doesn't race the
removal of the directory it is still writing to.

The bundle cites ``frame:N`` throughout; without this endpoint an HTTP
